verdict: Avoid new footwear exposure in Vellore-Ambur for now; lend only to Relaxo/Bata-anchored component suppliers with clean GST and tight monthly stock reporting, and decline unanchored job-work units.
title: Vellore-Ambur Footwear: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What this business physically is
**Footwear here is a low-capex assembly and job-work trade: cutting, lasting, stitching and packing for brand owners, plus small own-label units selling through local distributors.** Cash comes in when a brand or distributor lifts finished pairs; it goes out upfront for soles, uppers, adhesives and wages. The industry 'does not have a capital-intensive manufacturing process and hence the entry barriers of new players remain low' [7], so margins sit with whoever holds the brand, not the unit. **Assume thin conversion margins and price-taking behaviour unless the borrower owns a label.**

## Where cash and value sit now
**The value chain is recovering at the brand end but the recovery is distributor-led, not factory-led.** Relaxo's distributor count rose from 550 to 630 in one quarter and management said stock 'has been liquidated through the pipeline' after GST moved from 12% to 5% [1]. Relaxo Q4 FY26 revenue was INR751 crore, up 8.1%, EBITDA margin 16.5% [2]; Bata's Q1FY27 net profit rose 23% to Rs 64 crore [3]. **But Relaxo's full-year FY26 revenue was Rs 2,702 crore, down 3.1% [4] — a weak year with one good quarter.** So when a proposal lands, check whether the borrower's order book is a genuine new-season programme or a one-quarter restock; if the buyer is a distributor, ask for the brand's purchase order, not the distributor's. ## What has changed, and the local picture
**The local signal is negative and the sources say almost nothing specific about Vellore-Ambur — lean on first principles and the peers.** Tamil Nadu GST collections are -3.2% Apr-to-date against India +6.1% [D], and India-wide exports are -3.0% in USD [D]. Repo is 5.5% with a tightening stance [D], while IIP for leather/footwear (NIC 15) is +8.1% [D] — output is rising into softer local demand. **That combination means inventory will sit longer on small units' books.** Note the rating reports are undated or old (one is December 2024 [7]); treat them as structure guidance, not current performance. ## Who to pursue, who to avoid
**Pursue tier-2 component suppliers and job-workers with a named brand anchor, and franchisee/retail traders with owned or long-lease premises.** Ajanta-type models show 116 showrooms with 112 rented and 49 franchisees [5], and GCA of Rs 31.14 crore against repayment of Rs 4.18 crore [5] — that is the shape of a lendable retail borrower. **Avoid unanchored own-label units, pure trading intermediaries, and any unit whose sales depend on one distributor.** Stiff unorganised competition and low entry barriers [7] mean such units have no pricing power and no exit value. ## How to grow safely
**Structure against the stock, not the balance sheet story.** Fund working capital against verified finished-goods and receivable stock, take monthly GST returns and stock statements, and require the brand purchase order as the drawing-power base. Capex for plant and machinery should be matched to a confirmed order, since sector growth needs plant investment but debt-heavy players are 'more vulnerable to slowdown' [8]. ## Early-warning signs
**Watch the buyer mix and the stock turn, not the P&L.** A rising share of sales to a single distributor, stock ageing past one season, or GST turnover falling below bank-statement credits are the first cracks. If the borrower's main brand shifts to another vendor, the unit has no fallback — act on the first missed stock statement.
watch: gap above 10% for two months -> freeze limit, inspect stock
stock older than one season -> revalue drawing power, demand repayment
order book falls below last season -> downgrade and seek collateral
